Based on theoretical predictions, the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay process is used to determine the effective $B^0_s$-lifespan. This lifespan is influenced by $B^0_s$-meson mixing and its related mass and width differences. In the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ channel, the effective $B^0_s$-lifespan is assessed by analyzing the time sequence between particle production and decay. This analysis is performed on $66.4$ TeV of proton-proton collision data collected by the LHCb detector at the LHC. The $B^0_s$-meson lifespan and mixing-related parameters are incorporated into a simulation to determine their effect on the observed data. The analysis yields an effective $B^0_s$-lifespan of 1.176±0.014 (statistical uncertainty)±0.014 (systematic uncertainty) ps, which corresponds to a $B^0_s$-meson mixing-related parameter of 0.802±0.014 (statistical uncertainty)±0.014 (systematic uncertainty).

This research focuses on a discrete version of a system dynamics issue, which involves ensuring that the output of each component in a network remains within a specified range. The system is modeled using linear components that interact with one another in a linear fashion, and output beyond the range leads to increased components in the network. We analyze the stability of this system across a range of discrete time steps, and our findings show that the system remains stable under certain conditions, which are verified through numerical simulations. Our results also highlight the importance of choosing the right time step size to ensure the long-term sustainability of the network.

A study of the extreme highest-energy cosmic ray events recorded at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant fluctuations in their arrival times over vast areas of the sky spanning several years. By leveraging the site's extensive surface array, researchers were able to pinpoint the energy and arrival time of each event, and in some cases, their direction and energy distribution. The analysis of the fluctuations in both the total deposited energy and the isotropy of the sky shows that they are primarily a result of individual extreme events rather than a combination of many less energetic ones. Furthermore, the study of the fluctuations in the magnetic field induced by the arriving particles reveals that their magnitude is influenced by both the number of particles and the properties of the intergalactic medium. The study suggests that the observed magnetic field fluctuations are consistent with the intergalactic medium's properties and may provide valuable insights into the nature of the highest-energy cosmic rays.

We establish that any Zinbiel algebra whose underlying vector space is abelian must itself be an abelian structure, thereby confirming a previously conjectured property. This finding is related to the dual nature of free nth Lie-coloring algebras and extends the Zassenhaus basis theorem to the nth level.

Researchers have utilized the ALICE detector at the LHC to investigate the variations in particle flow direction and intensity within lead-lead collisions at a high energy level of 5.02 TeV. By analyzing the fluctuations in particle flow direction and intensity, they found that these variations are linked to the geometry of collisions and the initial positions of particles. The study found that the correlations between these fluctuations and the geometry of collisions are consistent with theoretical predictions. The study also found that the variation in particle intensity is higher than the variation in geometry of collisions, and that the initial positions of particles contribute significantly to these fluctuations. The study found that the variation in particle intensity is higher in central collisions than in peripheral collisions, and that the variation in particle intensity is influenced by the initial positions of particles. The study found that the variation in particle intensity is higher in central collisions than in peripheral collisions, and that the variation in particle intensity is influenced by the initial positions of particles.

This research focuses on resolving inconsistencies in relational tables, specifically those containing null values and functional dependencies. We define a discrepancy between two cells in the same row as a discrepancy between their values, given a particular dependency. We explore different approaches to address these discrepancies, including a method that prioritizes non-null values and a new approach called the "contextual approach." This new approach considers the surrounding cells' values to determine which cells' values to modify in order to resolve discrepancies. We develop an efficient algorithm to identify a set of contextually-aware discrepancies, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approaches through experiments.

This research introduces a novel regression model called the Time-Varying Poisson Autoregressive (TVPAR) model to address dynamic discrete regression problems. Building on the Poisson log-linear framework, the TVPAR model captures the temporal dependencies in the explanatory variables and response variable by allowing the autoregressive coefficients to change over time. The study develops the maximum likelihood estimation method for the TVPAR model and establishes the estimator's asymptotic properties. To compare the performance of the estimators, the research conducts a comprehensive Monte Carlo experiment. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the standard maximum likelihood estimation in estimating the true parameters. The study also applies the TVPAR model to real-world data, specifically analyzing the relationship between unemployment rates and GDP growth in the US and the impact of US-Germany interest rate differentials on the Euro/Dollar exchange rate.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDF), a novel approach for representing 3D objects that is robust to changes in viewpoint and orientation. NDF achieves this by utilizing a point cloud's local geometry to train a neural network, which outputs a 3D voxel space where each voxel contains a descriptor. This representation is particularly effective for robot manipulation tasks, as it allows the robot to retrieve past demonstrations based on their spatial relationship to a target object, regardless of orientation. We demonstrate the practical application of NDF in two distinct scenarios: data pose generalization and shared embedding space learning, both of which involve matching query and demonstration point clouds. The results of these experiments show that our approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art in data pose generalization and enables the creation of a shared embedding space between 2D and 3D representations.

Researchers have developed a Monte Carlo method to determine the precise value of the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity in classical systems exhibiting O(N) universality. Utilizing classical simulations of these systems, they found that the real part of the critical point is positioned at $-1.90333(25)$ for a one-dimensional case and $-0.48363(10)$ for a two-dimensional case across various N values. These results have been compared to previously established results and theoretical predictions, and a new set of critical exponents has been derived from the simulations.

In this work, we establish a lemma that extends the comparison technique for sums of random variables introduced by Altug and Wagner, specifically for stochastic approximation in the context of the spherical model. This lemma allows us to achieve two main achievements. First, we provide a shorter proof of the Sudakov and Temme comparison of the update functions within the AMP framework. This enables us to replicate the primary result from an associated paper. Second, we derive the local concavity of the TAP free energy, as well as the corresponding stochastic update behavior beyond any fixed length scale. This second achievement relies solely on the lemma and does not utilize the AMP comparison technique.

A new aerosol assessment framework is introduced, building on a well-known method for determining clear sky atmospheric turbulence. This framework utilizes images from astronomical photometry to analyze aerosol properties. The process involves three main stages: first, it identifies and selects only clear sky images from a large image set. The authors present a new, more efficient algorithm for identifying these images. The selected images are then used to create a lungard regression model that accurately predicts clear sky images from others. This model is trained and validated using images from various astronomical surveys. The results indicate that the model can effectively identify clear sky images with high precision and recall. The final stage of the framework applies the trained model to images from weather-sensitive observations to detect and map high-altitude thin cirrus clouds. The researchers found that these clouds are prevalent in certain regions, particularly in the southwestern United States, and are often undetectable in infrared images. The proposed framework demonstrates the potential of using astronomical imaging to provide a comprehensive assessment of atmospheric aerosols. This capability can be leveraged to enhance various fields, including astronomy, atmospheric science, and climate research.

To accurately estimate the complete six-degree-of-freedom pose of objects from images, it is essential to incorporate information about how projected points relate to one another. This study focuses on utilizing this relational knowledge to improve pose estimation, developing a novel framework that combines a Projection Grouping Network and a Correspondence Transformer. Initially, during training, the network identifies clusters of projected points that correspond to distinct object parts, and subsequently, a correspondence transformer is employed to capture the relationship between these clusters and the observed image, facilitating precise pose prediction. Furthermore, a dual-stream design is introduced to handle both clustered and unclustered points, and an adaptive loss function is created to address the challenge of sparse point matching. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, achieving superior performance compared to existing methods.

We present GGLasso, a Python-based tool designed for Generalized Graphical Lasso estimation, which identifies the most effective structure among high-dimensional datasets by focusing on conditional independence relationships. This lattice problem is complex and can be resolved using a combination of the sparse Cholesky decomposition and sparse inverse thresholding methods. GGLasso includes features such as automatic hyperparameter selection, multiple loss function options, and visualization capabilities, along with extensive documentation and testing.

A key challenge in simulating complex molecules is accurately modeling their three-dimensional structure and molecular movements. Standard methods for this involve calculating the arrangement of molecules based on statistical physics principles. However, these methods can struggle to produce reliable results due to the computationally intensive nature of these calculations. In this study, we developed a new algorithm that uses molecular dynamics to generate accurate and stable models of molecules in three-dimensional space. This new approach is highly efficient, reducing computation time by up to 100 times compared to existing methods while also producing more reliable results. Our algorithm's performance was tested on a range of molecules, from small peptides to large protein complexes, and it outperformed the current state-of-the-art in terms of both computation time and accuracy.

As complex systems evolve from simple to multi-layered representations, traditional methods of analyzing and ranking their components are becoming inadequate. We've developed a novel approach called Node Prominence (NP) to evaluate and prioritize components within a multi-layered network by identifying the most significant layer and applying the Eigenvector Prominence (EP) method. NP incorporates a new metric, Node Centrality (NC), to assess the importance of components within each layer. We've applied this approach to a three-layered network derived from the interactions between the US, Russia, and China in the Ukraine crisis, revealing that internal dynamics within Russia's network play a pivotal role in shaping the conflict. We've also explored the impact of varying network connections on NP results, providing a framework for analyzing complex, evolving conflicts.

Recently, the fundamental commutation rules for $R$-Minkowski spacetime were established, enabling the creation of a Schr\"odinger-like equation. This new framework allows for the derivation of the $R$-Minkowski version of Dirac's equation. When transformed back to standard spacetime, it accurately reverts to the conventional Dirac equation.

Spherical droplets or partial droplets formed on flat surfaces are widely used in microfluidics and other applications. However, their performance is significantly influenced by how they are created. Recently, a method called LESS was developed to generate high-quality spherical droplets on flat surfaces. In this study, researchers examined whether this method works effectively for solid spheres moving from a liquid pool to a solid surface. By analyzing the behavior of spheres during the LESS process using computational fluid dynamics, they identified key parameters that influence the process and its outcome. Their findings showed that a new dimensionless number, which is specific to the LESS process, is an important factor in determining the success of the process. Furthermore, they derived a new relationship for this process, which can be used to predict the conditions under which spheres can be created successfully. This study also has implications for other processes that involve the creation of spherical shapes on flat surfaces.

In the context of string theory, a specific subset of the full supergravity theory is examined, which exhibits global symmetries and allows for nonperturbative axion-dilaton couplings of the form $e^{-S_{\rm inst}}$. Within this theory, the nonperturbative contributions to the $\theta$-term are found to be governed by the universal $\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ duality group, which acts on the axion-dilaton field. The analysis of the string and M-theory instantons reveals that they contribute to the $\theta$-term in distinct manners.

The electronic structure of cupricite exhibits a wide range of interesting properties, including a unique, partially filled d-orbital that gives rise to its distinctive color. Although its spectral characteristics have been well-documented, the underlying origin of one of its absorption peaks remains unclear. Using advanced theoretical methods, we have investigated the electronic structure of cupricite and found that this mysterious peak is a result of the localized d-orbital, which arises due to strong electron interactions. We have also discovered that these interactions lead to the formation of an energy gap between the filled d-orbital and the conduction band, which is composed of copper's filled s-orbital. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the d-orbital of the cupricite is highly sensitive to temperature, leading to an asymmetric distribution of electrons between the two metal ions in the material.

In this research, we investigate the phenomenon of Rabi oscillations in an exciton system without the presence of an external magnetic field. We find that Rabi frequencies can be directly correlated to the strength of the light-matter interaction. Notably, we demonstrate that Rabi frequencies can be controlled by adjusting the thickness of the material. We also derive an expression for the effective light-matter interaction Hamiltonian and use it to simulate the system's behavior under various conditions. Our simulations reveal that Rabi oscillations can occur over extremely short time scales, as small as 10 picoseconds in certain materials. We further explore the impact of an external magnetic field on the system and find that Rabi frequencies can be significantly altered, allowing for the coherent manipulation of the system's quantum states.

Our research examines the electronic band structure of a 2D beta-brass structure lattice, which exhibits strong symmorphic character in its space group. By applying a periodic potential, we discovered that the lattice can be made non-symmorphic, and we observed that its $K$ points behave like ordinary crossing points that lack cone shape characteristics. We observed that these points can move linearly in response to changes in lattice parameters, and we even managed to eliminate their presence by adjusting the system's periodicity. We also found that these points display different behaviors when subjected to perpendicular and parallel periodic potentials, and we believe that this discovery could have significant implications for the field of electronics.

Quantum states that span multiple length scales, known as Fock-state superpositions, are highly beneficial for various quantum technologies. Single-photon facilitated coherent states (SFS) represent a novel type of superposition with unique properties, exhibiting an inherent tendency to emit single photons and offering inherent protection against photon loss. Although previous methods for generating SFS rely on post-selection, this approach is inefficient. A more effective approach is proposed in this study, utilizing quantum-optical catalysis to produce pure SFS without the need for post-selection. This method involves a $\chi^{(2)}$ non-linear crystal and demonstrates that the produced state's purity can be tuned by adjusting specific parameters. Furthermore, the proposed scheme is adaptable to other states that require post-selection, by changing the non-linear interaction.

In the context of General Relativity, we will employ the Newman-Penrose formalism to analyze a specific type of object, namely a bivector, represented by an antisymmetric tensor with four components. We will begin by examining the representation of the electromagnetic field using this object, and then proceed to depict the Riemann tensor within the vacuum field equations. Notably, the bivector has no direct representation within the Newman-Penrose formalism, and as a result, it is necessary to utilize two 'null bases' for its depiction. Ultimately, we will demonstrate the decomposition of the Riemann tensor into its various parts, including the Ricci tensor, the scalar curvature, and the Weyl curvature matrix, and we will illustrate how the components of this matrix can be derived from the bivector.

This research presents a novel approach to discovering molecular compounds within a specified class of formulas, employing a technique that combines the analysis of existing compounds' data with optimization methods. By treating molecules as mathematical structures and utilizing a matrix to represent their atomic compositions, the team developed a strategy to identify molecules that correspond to a target structure through the determination of a coefficient matrix. This technique was applied to identify molecular compounds within a structure related to polymeric lithium electrolytes, resulting in a set of thirteen previously unreported formulas with lithium content ranging from 11.1% to 22.2%. These novel molecules were further analyzed through theoretical modeling of their physical and thermal characteristics.

Segmenting tumors in the esophagus from computed tomography scans is a difficult task due to the low contrast between the tumor and surrounding tissue, as well as the varying shape and size of the neoplasm. In this paper, we present a novel deep learning model, DDAUnet, for automatically segmenting esophageal neoplasms in CT images. DDAUnet is based on a 3D U-Net architecture and incorporates several key components, including dense connections, attention mechanisms, and dilated convolutions, to improve segmentation accuracy. We pre-trained DDAUnet using a Dense UNet, fine-tuned it with a 3D U-Net, and added attention mechanisms and dilated convolutions to capture the spatial and semantic information of the images. Our model was evaluated on two publicly available datasets, and achieved higher Dice Similarity Coefficients (DSC) than other state-of-the-art methods. DDAUnet is a highly effective and efficient model for automatically segmenting esophageal neoplasms in CT images.

Multilingual individuals frequently blend different languages within a single sentence or sentence group, a phenomenon known as code-switching or code-mixing. Although this behavior presents significant challenges for NLP systems, understanding the underlying factors is crucial for developing effective multilingual solutions. This study provides a thorough examination of the linguistic and technical aspects influencing code-mixing, covering areas such as orthographic compatibility, phonetic similarity, semantic relatedness, and domain-specific mixing patterns. By analyzing these influences, we aim to offer actionable insights for creating more effective multilingual NLP solutions. To facilitate this, we developed a dataset called CROWD-MIX, consisting of over 10,000 naturally occurring code-mixed sentences in English and Hindi. To further encourage the creation of code-mixed datasets, we also created a Python tool called MixIt, which can be used to combine parallel datasets into code-mixed versions. To illustrate the practical applications of this technology, we used CROWD-MIX to train a multilingual variant of BERT that outperforms monolingual BERT models on various natural language processing tasks.

Utilizing human refences, such as descriptions in visual tasks, has been effective for improving model performance. We investigate whether human references can enhance the evaluation of image descriptions. We employ the MS-COCO description set for training and assessment on multiple evaluation metrics, including those based on sequences and a newly created human-centric metric. The results indicate that simple integration of human references can improve the reliability of automatic assessment methods, aligning them more closely with human judgment. This finding holds true across different datasets and metrics, suggesting a cost-effective means of improving image description evaluation.

Tantalum oxide with the Ta$_2$O$_5$ composition is a complex material that exhibits multiple crystal forms, and its unique properties make it suitable for various applications, including supercapacitors, gas sensors, and photodetectors. The base state structure of this material remains unknown, and its accurate characterization is crucial for a deeper understanding of its characteristics. In this study, researchers are attempting to identify and characterize the base state structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ by using advanced computational techniques. They have utilized density functional theory and stochastic simulations to determine the material's base state crystal structure, and found that it is characterized by a distorted cubic symmetry and belongs to the space group P2$_3$. Furthermore, they have also characterized the material's electronic and magnetic properties, and determined that it is an insulator with a moderate band gap of 2.8 eV and exhibits paramagnetism. The Ta$_2$O$_5$ material is also highly stable and resistant to structural changes, and its unique properties make it an interesting material for further study.

Reddit's subreddits are organized into a geographic hierarchy, with cities and states having their own dedicated subreddits and associated directories known as "geographic sorts." Despite their practical purpose, researchers have not thoroughly examined their effects on information dissemination. This study focuses on the most extensive geographic sort, the United States sort, to investigate how it influences the spread of both accurate and false information among users of various Reddit platforms. Our findings reveal that users who have a higher likelihood of interacting with the U.S. sort are 10% less likely to share false information and 10% more likely to spread accurate information. Furthermore, we discovered that the reduced risk of encountering false information within the geographic sort is the primary driver behind these results. The study also explores alternative explanations, including the impact of political affiliation and the geographic sort's effect on users' perceptions of their own location.

Verbal guidance from human instructors is an essential aspect of demonstration learning, yet there is still limited understanding of the linguistic patterns used during such instruction. To bridge this knowledge gap, we investigate the speech characteristics of a human instructor who was previously recorded during the performance of a robotic instruction task. We analyzed the speech data from five human instructors, including the one in question, and discovered that the instructors' speech patterns are quite similar to each other. Furthermore, we found that the speech patterns exhibited by the instructors are more complex than what can be captured by traditional statistical methods. We also observed that the speech patterns of the specific instructor in question are more straightforward than the rest. Moreover, we found that the speech patterns exhibited during instruction are more complex than those during non-instructional tasks. These findings provide a foundation for the development of models that incorporate verbal information in learning from demonstrations.

The intricate behavior of irrational second-level polynomial conformal field theories is investigated through the lens of the dynamical Euler-Arnold equations, revealing a direct correspondence between the theory's irrationality and the chaotic behavior of the equations. This research reveals that the correlation functions in irrational second-level polynomial CFTs exhibit stochastic properties akin to random walks, and the Liouville one-point function in the natural vacuum state reveals a self-similar pattern.

Conversational systems are increasingly used in customer service, and they're expected to handle complex, multi-step dialogues. To ensure these systems effectively manage such dialogues, rigorous testing methods are necessary. However, current automated testing tools lack the sophistication of human testers, which limits their ability to accurately evaluate these advanced applications. This paper introduces a novel framework for creating machine testing systems that can handle complex, multi-step dialogues. The proposed system leverages existing conversational testers and pre-made conversation scripts, and is demonstrated using an actual application built with the Dialogflow platform. The effectiveness of this system is validated through a case study, showing its ability to detect issues in various parts of a dialogues, including the introduction, execution, and closing stages. The source code for this system is available online at https://github.com/alejandro-ortiz/machine-testing-system-for-conversational-bots.

Recommending users based on data from multiple sparse domains presents a significant challenge due to the limited information available in each domain. While various methods have been explored to improve recommendations, existing approaches have primarily focused on sharing information across domains, neglecting the distinct characteristics of each domain. In response, we introduce a novel approach called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSD-CR), which leverages the unique properties of each domain to benefit others. Specifically, we propose learning comprehensive preference representations for each domain, incorporating both dense and sparse components. By utilizing the unique characteristics of each domain, we enable domains with limited information to draw upon the rich information available in other domains. Experimental results on three real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in terms of recommendation accuracy.

This research focuses on resolving natural conic representations of various mathematical problems within the hyperelliptic realm. We utilize the Software Development Kit for Convex Optimization in Julia, specifically Hypatia, to address and analyze these expressions. Our investigation reveals that a fundamental problem's representation as a second-order conic problem is straightforward, whereas more intricate problems require a larger dimensional space to solve. Our findings also highlight the impact of dimensional space on the size of natural representations and the efficiency of solving these problems, with our results made available on the arXiv platform.

In recent years, large-scale medical imaging datasets have grown significantly, enabling the use of deep learning techniques for various image analysis tasks. However, a major challenge remains: ensuring that trained models produce reliable outputs. Traditional quality control methods have limitations due to their slow speed and inability to generalize across different imaging modalities. In this study, we investigate the underlying causes of these generalization difficulties using quality assurance datasets from human brain MRIs. We find that multiple, complex and interacting factors contribute to the models' performance limitations, including image resolution, distortion levels, and signal-to-noise ratios. Our research highlights the need to consider these variables jointly in order to develop more effective quality assurance tools that can generalize well across different imaging conditions.

As the use of private electric vehicles increases, their impact on power grid reliability during extreme weather events is a growing concern. This study focuses on quantifying grid resilience in the face of weather-related disasters and developing strategies to improve it. By employing the concept of service restoration speed, we establish a quantitative framework for resilience that considers the recovery of both the power grid and its connected vehicles. A simulation platform is created to model interactions between grid operators and vehicle owners during a disaster, utilizing a multi-agent reinforcement learning approach to optimize charging behavior. This optimization aims to minimize energy costs and maximize the speed of grid recovery. Through numerical analysis, we gain insights into the influence of private electric vehicles on grid resilience and the effectiveness of coordinated charging in achieving this goal.

A Drive-In Meeting is a novel social gathering where participants, from friends to acquaintances, meet in their cars within an enclosed area, engaging in conversations without stepping out of their vehicles. Recently, this concept has gained popularity due to heightened health concerns. To explore strategies for successfully organizing such events, a paper titled "Multi-Agent Recurrent Drive-In Meeting Incentive" introduces a dynamic scenario where participants decide whether to attend, the duration of attendance, and the conversation topics to discuss. A game theory approach is employed to analyze this situation, treating conversation topics as public goods that can be influenced by contributions. A time-dependent model is developed to represent this dynamic situation, and it is simplified to a one-shot game for analysis. Results indicate the existence of various equilibrium outcomes, including scenarios where attendees benefit from the events and situations involving conversation free-riding. A simulation demonstrates the one-shot model's applicability to the dynamic scenario, and suggestions for incentivizing participation and attendance are proposed to facilitate multi-agent recurrent events.

This research delves into the structural, electronic and magnetic properties of GdSn3, CmSn3 and the solid solution Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn3 using a first-principles approach within the DFT framework. The calculations were performed using the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method. Our results show that GdSn3 and CmSn3 exhibit a cubic crystal structure with space group $Fm\bar3m$ and display antiferromagnetic behavior. The calculations reveal that GdSn3 is a metallic material, whereas CmSn3 behaves as a semimetal. The analysis of the electronic and magnetic characteristics indicates that the d and f orbitals of Gd and the s and p orbitals of Sn are primarily responsible for the metallic nature of GdSn3. Furthermore, GdSn3 exhibits a magnetic moment of 6.9 $\mu_B$, whereas CmSn3 has a reduced magnetic moment of 4.8 $\mu_B$. The analysis of Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn3 indicates that the magnetic moment of these compounds is directly proportional to the Gd concentration.
A table is compiled that projects extra baryon and meson content beyond equilibrium states, drawing on recent research and relevant sources.

A key component in Euclidean geometry is the Fano theorem, which has a proof that relies on the properties of vectors. In a non-Archimedean setting, the Fano theorem's proof can be derived using vector space principles. However, the Coxeter group $K$ has a more complex geometric structure than a vector space, making it unclear whether the foundation theorem for B-type groups, proven by Tignol and Amour, can be simplified using the same approach. In this study, we establish a "generalized foundation theorem" that encompasses the Tignol-Amour theorem and the fano theorem, both of which can be seen as specific instances. By doing so, we develop a more straightforward proof for the Tignol-Amour theorem.

Researchers have long debated the influence of cosmology on Type Ia supernovae observed through weak lensing effects. To address this, we have developed a new method for identifying these supernovae by utilizing the color variations in their light curves and have applied this technique to the Pantheon sample of 1050 Type Ia supernovae. Our analysis reveals that the lensing-induced magnification biases in the Pantheon sample's distance modulus and dark energy parameter estimates amount to 0.003 and 0.015, respectively. Although these figures are beyond the measurements' precision, they serve as significant benchmarks for future, more precise cosmological studies.

T-shaped waveguide junctions are commonly used in photonic integrated circuits, and their behavior is influenced by the geometry of their junction region. We investigated how the junction design impacts the transmission efficiency of T-junctions made in silicon-on-insulator technology at a wavelength of 1550nm. Our research revealed that a specific geometry, featuring a junction with a 100nm depth and 500nm width, exhibited the highest transmission efficiency, surpassing 99%. Notably, this design maintained a consistent transmission efficiency of above 99% across a 20nm wavelength range.

The human capacity to comprehend object placement within its environment is a key differentiator from current deep learning-based object recognition systems. In contrast to these systems, we can leverage spatial relationships to enhance the robustness of our object detectors. We propose a straightforward, yet effective method to evaluate the degree of appropriateness of an image's context for its primary object. Our approach involves utilizing a simple point cloud network to assess the surrounding environment and a state-of-the-art object detector to provide confidence scores. This hybrid system's performance is assessed on the MS COCO dataset, and it outperforms random context selection by a significant margin. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that our network can identify instances of inappropriate object placement and the majority of challenging images with difficult or ambiguous contexts. We make our code available for public use at https://github.com/andrewjia/context_for_cocr.

We examine the conditions under which a collection of binary random variables that are correlated in opposite directions satisfy a specific concentration inequality, similar to Hoeffding's inequality for independent random variables. Our analysis yields a set of criteria, and we demonstrate how these criteria apply to various types of data, including binary matrices with constrained column and row sums, and adjacency matrices of unweighted graphs that do not contain certain edge configurations.

In the context of mirror symmetry, a natural question arises: can any given symplectic manifold be transformed to achieve Calabi-Yau properties through a specific type of modification known as a symplectic blow-up? This study delves into the fundamental properties of such alterations, exploring their behavior under calibration and the preservation of key features like Kaehler structure and Fano properties. It is demonstrated that Calabi-Yau characteristics remain intact after a blow-up in the symplectic category, whereas the set of Fano symplectic manifolds is reduced. Moreover, the study reveals that the collection of symplectic manifolds with a fixed first Chern class is not closed under the operation of a specific type of alteration, in contrast to the more flexible Chern classes of Kaehler manifolds following a similar alteration, as shown by Hodge theory.

A crucial issue in kidney transplantation is the mismatch between donor and recipient immune systems, which is measured by the HLA mismatch. Historically, compatibility was determined by the number of mismatched antigens, but a more precise method, the calculated panel reactive T-cell (cPRA), assesses compatibility by comparing the proportion of potential donors that a recipient is incompatible with. This study examines the relationship between HLA mismatch and the likelihood of a successful kidney transplant, measured by graft survival. Using data from 10,000 transplants in the United States between 2005 and 2014, we found that a lower cPRA mismatch is associated with better graft survival. This effect is most pronounced in the first year after the transplant and is more significant for certain types of mismatches. This study provides evidence that cPRA mismatch is a meaningful indicator of incompatibility and may be useful in evaluating the acceptance of kidneys that are not a perfect match.

We investigate whether the word representations of four popular text embedding techniques can capture the semantic meaning of positive and negative sentiment words from the Loughran-McDonald dictionary, specifically tailored for the financial sector. Using established comprehend scores, we find that representation vectors for words such as "profit," "asset," "gain," and "loss," "undervalued," and "overvalued" do possess a degree of semantic understanding of sentiment. Notably, we discovered that the strategy of taking the difference between the vector values of singular and plural forms of a word can significantly enhance the comprehensibility of its sentiment semantics, particularly for words like "undervalued" and "overvalued." We also provide a comprehensive analysis of the relationship between a word's sentiment semantics and its morphological, phonological, and orthographic characteristics.

This work derives the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based models for an IPT system, which utilizes multiple antennas and OFDM, in order to provide a fair comparison of performance. A conversion formula is also developed to convert the specific IPT loss model parameters into an OFDM equivalent, enabling a direct comparison. These equivalent models are useful tools for evaluating the performance of multi-coil SISO IPT systems in real-world wireless environments.

This research presents an approach to modeling solidification and melting in fluids by combining the level-set method with an embedded boundary technique. The level-set method is used to derive a precise interface reconstruction, enabling a more accurate representation of the boundary in a numerical simulation. The governing equation is discretized using a second-order finite difference method on a Cartesian grid, with an efficient multigrid solver employed to handle the operator. The researcher presents a modified normal computation technique to ensure a conservative numerical solution. The approach is validated through a series of numerical experiments, including the Stefan problem with temperature-dependent properties and the Rayleigh-B\'enard problem with surface tension effects. The results obtained through this technique are found to be highly accurate and reliable.

In multiplayer competitions, a player's success hinges on their ability to accurately predict their opponents' moves. We investigate the conditions under which these predictions can be rationalizable equilibria, a concept that encompasses Nash equilibria but also includes a broader class of solution concepts. Our primary contribution is a set of efficient algorithms for acquiring strategy profiles that correspond to the points of rationalizable equilibria in both simultaneous and sequential games. These algorithms are designed to operate in polynomial time with respect to the size of the game's payoff space, a critical factor in real-world applications. We also provide a detailed analysis of the size of the rationalizable equilibria set, a concept that has not been previously explored. Our framework is flexible enough to accommodate a range of learning dynamics, including those based on best responses and regret minimization, and we demonstrate how to acquire rationalizable equilibria in multiplayer simultaneous games and extensive-form games in both constant and logarithmic external queries.

This research analyzes the transmission of a stochastic disease through an electrical power grid that experiences a sudden, unplanned change, specifically the removal of a compromised node and its associated connections. We examine how the temporary removal of a node affected by the disease, along with its connections, influences the spread of infection within the system. Our study focuses on the effects of this proactive measure on both susceptible and infected nodes, taking into consideration the timing of node removal. We found that delaying node removal can lead to an increase in the overall spread of infection, as it allows for the removal of more infected nodes, but also results in the removal of more susceptible nodes that could have been saved. Our analysis reveals that the timing of node removal plays a crucial role in preventing the spread of infection, and that this proactive measure can be an effective strategy for protecting vulnerable populations. Our study also highlights the limitations of this approach and the need for further research to develop more effective strategies for preventing the spread of infection in complex systems.

This paper presents a structured approach to creating a statistical model for particle physics, focusing on the specific task of determining the parton distribution functions (PDFs) in hadrons. We begin by outlining the fundamental equations and concepts, and then outline the specific calculations required to make a numerical model that can be compared to experimental data. This involves breaking down the various components of the measured cross sections into their contributing parts, each with its own PDF dependence. As the order of calculations increases in QCD, the number of relevant processes to consider grows, and we also need to account for the effects of higher twists and other corrections. The framework we describe is designed to be easily adaptable to the specific needs of PDF fitting programs, and we illustrate its application by considering the determination of the strange quark distribution in the proton.

Reinforcement learning agents in complex environments often struggle due to limited data, as they must infer optimal behavior from their initial policy. To overcome this limitation, researchers have proposed using a better-performing policy to select data for data replay, but this approach has a drawback: the resulting dataset becomes increasingly biased towards certain parts of the state space, leading to the agent focusing too much on those areas. In this work, we investigate this issue and develop a new algorithm, Policy-VarDCE, that controls the diversity of the replayed data to prevent it from becoming too narrow. We evaluate our approach on various tasks and find that it outperforms existing methods, particularly in difficult scenarios, while maintaining a balanced exploration of the state space.

In our study, we present a large-scale, complex conversation dataset consisting of over 10,000 conversations, each with an average of 19 turns and more than 100 branching points. This dataset, known as MultiTalk, is designed to support a range of dialogue research applications, including the examination of language, spoken language understanding, and conversation management. We found that models trained on the initial parts of these conversations struggled to predict subsequent content, indicating the difficulty of the dataset. Moreover, we observed that more intricate, interconnected conversations were more challenging to predict, understand, and manage than linear conversations. This analysis highlights the need for research into the control aspects of spoken conversations. We provide easy-to-use documentation and code to facilitate the use of this dataset.

We have developed a novel, efficient method for simulating the dynamics of large-scale cosmic structures in various modified gravity theories with multiple types of matter interactions. Our approach utilizes a specific mathematical transformation to simplify these simulations by decoupling certain species from gravitational effects and coupling others in distinct ways. This pseudo-linear accuracy allows for simulating $10^9$ bodies within a cubic gigaparsec using $10^7$ computational cores, achieving a significant leap in computational efficiency. Our algorithm seamlessly integrates with existing simulation tools like GADGET and can be used to produce high-accuracy, rapid N-body simulations for a range of modified gravity models, including those with scalar-tensor and $f(R)$ gravity interactions. Our new method generates significantly more detailed and accurate data than previous approaches in much less time, offering a substantial improvement in computational efficiency and accuracy.

We establish that the imaginary part of any unit interval of the complex plane, given a Gaussian free field on the plane with boundary conditions, defines a region whose boundary consists of a collection of non-intersecting curves. These curves, which do not overlap, are found to be equivalent in distribution to curves from Schramm-Loewner evolution with a specific parameter value, conditioned to avoid each other. Additionally, we derive the exact parameters governing these SLE curves from their corresponding driving processes in the log-gas framework.

We introduce WorkingWiki, a collaborative research tool built on top of MediaWiki, which we developed and launched in response to the need for a collaborative platform during the COVID-19 pandemic. WorkingWiki enables a group of researchers to co-edit and organize subject-specific content, much like a dynamic, growing set of lecture notes. We describe the key features of WorkingWiki that make it suitable for this purpose, and we discuss the benefits and limitations of using such a system. We also discuss the potential applications of WorkingWiki in various fields, including its current use in astroparticle physics. We make the source code of WorkingWiki available on GitHub at https://github.com/AstroPPTT/WorkingWiki.

This study develops a methodology to predict the fluid dynamics of a jet fire's combustion instability, taking into account combustion, through acoustic resonance within an enclosure. The approach combines theoretical and numerical techniques to solve the Rayleigh criterion, utilizing a high-fidelity numerical model based on the Large Eddy Simulation method to determine combustion effects. The results show that a detailed representation of combustion is essential for accurately predicting fluid dynamics and acoustic resonance within the enclosure. Furthermore, the study examines the impact of combustion modeling on the jet fire's combustion dynamics response to acoustic forcing through a linearized framework. The analysis also reveals the presence of hysteresis behavior and asymmetric response characteristics, along with initial conditions dependence, in the jet fire's reaction to acoustic forcing in a linearized framework. The research also compares the outcomes to previous studies on jet fire instabilities, demonstrating the applicability of a linearized approach for predicting combustion dynamics response to acoustic forcing at low to moderate amplitude levels. The study also proposes an efficient modeling technique, based on Active Flame Method, for predicting the combustion dynamics response to acoustic forcing in a linearized framework.

The interplay between neutrino $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay and ultralight dark matter is investigated in this study. We consider a scenario in which a neutrino interacts with a dark matter particle through an anapole coupling, leading to an anharmonic oscillation of the dark matter field and time-varying neutrino mass eigenvalues. This variation in mass eigenvalues can result in neutrinoless double beta decay, with the decay rate depending on the relationship between the dark matter mass and the neutrino mass scale. We also examine the impact of this interaction on neutrino cosmology, with the resulting neutrino dark matter interaction leading to an enhanced production of dark matter and a suppression of neutrinoless double beta decay. We derive the parameter space for the anapole coupling and dark matter mass scale that satisfies the neutrinoless double beta decay rate and cosmological constraints. We further explore the potential for neutrinoless double beta decay experiments to detect ultralight dark matter and the possibility of LISA detecting the dark matter signal. We also propose that the Neutrino Factory could produce a distinctive signature of ultralight dark matter.

A nonlocal gravitational theory is developed that incorporates a specific type of nonlocal connection, which is demonstrated to be equivalent to a general coordinate transformation. A specific example of this nonlocal connection is shown to be comparable to the connection used in the Poincar\'e gauge theory of gravity. A key distinction is identified between the two theories, as nonlinearity in nonlocal gravity is inherent, whereas in Poincar\'e gauge theory, it is artificially introduced. A nonlocal version of the theory is then derived that includes a specific type of intrinsic nonlinearity, which is shown to be analogous to a specific form of nonlocal gravity. A comparison is made with another nonlocal gravitational theory, highlighting the key differences between the two theories.

A comprehensive analysis of human traits was conducted by combining genomic enrichment data from functional annotations with results from genome-wide association studies (GWAS). This examination was carried out collaboratively by the Genetic Association and Expression group at the Broad Institute, involving 18 different traits analyzed through a specific set of 1800 non-coding annotations. The analysis focused on GWAS results from within the 1Mb regions that define these annotations, and the collaborative work spanned various categories of genomic features, including transcription factors, RNA, chromatin structure, and conservation. The examination utilized a standardized set of statistical methods, including fine-mapping, functional prioritization, and enrichment testing, across 20,000 individual GWAS files. The studied traits encompassed a wide range of human characteristics, such as blood pressure, cholesterol levels, lung function, Crohn's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, schizophrenia, type 2 diabetes, height, BMI, educational attainment, and several others. The results showed that annotations related to conserved non-coding sequences and specific chromatin states exhibited the highest levels of genomic enrichment, and the analysis also explored the impact of population-specific and tissue-specific annotations on these traits.

This thesis focuses on rare, high-transverse-momentum isolated photon and di-photon production in proton-proton collisions at a root-mean-square transverse momentum of 7 and 8 TeV. Our primary goal is to identify sources of impurity in these isolated photon and di-photon production processes. We examine various mechanisms that can lead to hadron emission, including semi-hard parton-shower effects, initial and final state radiation, and parton scattering. We also investigate the impact of underlying events and beam remnants on the isolation of photons. Our findings reveal that semi-hard parton-shower effects are the main contributors to hadron emission, with initial and final state radiation playing a secondary role. We determine that initial state radiation is more pronounced in di-photon production compared to isolated photon production. Our research shows that the underlying event and beam remnants have a minimal effect on the isolation of photons. Our results are applicable to isolated photon and di-photon production in LHC experiments.

The recurrence intervals of individual transient systems in the Milky Way's central region are found to be exponentially distributed, with a median recurrence period of 1000 years. This distribution is consistent with theoretical models of star formation near the Galactic Center, particularly those focusing on the migration and growth of massive young stellar objects. The study also compares the current distribution of quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Center to its past state, finding that the character of these systems has changed over time. The present-day distribution is dominated by long-period systems, whereas in the past, short-period systems were more prevalent. The study suggests that this shift is due to the preferential disruption of short-period systems by interactions with massive young stellar objects during the most recent 10^6 years.

A theoretical model has been developed to describe the coupling between an electron and vibrations in a crystal, taking into account the mass of electrons. This results in a new type of interaction that arises from the electrons' inertia and is distinct from the well-known linear electron-phonon coupling. The intensity of this new interaction is directly related to the frequency of the vibrations and is typically much stronger than linear coupling. This new interaction is universal and applies to all crystals, as it is not dependent on specific symmetries. A detailed examination of its effects on various aspects of solid-state physics has been conducted, including modifications to electron energy bands, the creation of localized states near band edges, and the formation of vibrational states filled with electrons.

We investigate semantic diversity in human conversations using Natural Language Inference (NLI), focusing on the semantic variety of utterances within a dialogue. Utilizing an annotated multi-turn dialogue dataset for Natural Inferencing Conversations (NICO), we introduce two novel tasks: predicting the validity of textentual entailment between adjacent dialogue turns and identifying the most suitable follow-up utterance based on a given dialogue. Our results show that consecutive utterances in a dialogue frequently exhibit entailment relationships, surpassing the frequency seen in single sentence pairs. Additionally, our end-to-end model for natural inferencing in conversations outperforms random selection baselines and comparable single-turn models, highlighting the potential of large language models to learn and apply semantic diversity in conversations. Our findings also emphasize the importance of semantic diversity in shaping the richness of language in conversations. NICO and related resources are publicly accessible at https://github.com/GegeXu/NICO.

The mass-shedding limit for rotating objects is the maximum rotation rate at which centrifugal force equals gravitational pull at the equator, causing the object to break apart. Understanding this limit is crucial for accurately interpreting the rotation of exoplanets, brown dwarfs, and other celestial bodies. However, the exact point of mass-shedding is still debated, with some studies suggesting that objects will start ejecting mass well before reaching the limit. To investigate this, we developed a computational model to examine the mass-shedding limit for rotating sub-stellar bodies with varying densities, using a 3D finite element method. Our model accounts for the effects of rotation on the object's shape and internal stress distribution, and it can handle the complex, non-linear behavior of the object's material. We found that the point of mass-shedding depends on the object's rotation axis and that it occurs at a significantly higher rotation rate than previously predicted. Our model also revealed that objects will experience localized material failure at the point of mass-shedding, with the extent of this failure depending on the object's material properties. We believe that our computational modeling provides a more accurate prediction of the mass-shedding limit for rotating sub-stellar bodies, and it can be used to better interpret observations of object shapes and internal structures.

To enhance the performance of our algorithm in matching simulated data with experimental observations, we've revised the initial estimation of the interference terms' coefficients. This involves employing a method of least squares to determine the coefficients that multiply the known electromagnetic form factors in the interference terms' expressions. By adjusting the number of considered processes and incorporating information from the total cross-section measurements, we've expanded our analysis. Our updated estimates successfully minimize discrepancies between our predictions and experimental data, as evidenced by reduced $\chi^2$ values in $\gamma p$ meson production processes such as $VPD$, $\rho$-meson, and $\pi$-meson production.

This research employs the radiation hydrodynamics approach to examine the decay patterns of gamma-ray burst (GRB) remnants during the phase following the peak of flux, utilizing an initial flux evolution model proposed by the author. The proposed model, which is based on an extensive analysis of existing empirical data, incorporates over 400 distinct events and aims to provide a comprehensive and straightforward explanation of observed trends in GRB flux evolution, including correlations between various time-delay parameters. The model successfully accounts for these correlations without relying on complex, interrelated coefficients. The author then investigates the relationships between time-delay parameters and the flux of the GRB remnants, demonstrating that the proposed model accurately predicts the characteristic decay patterns observed in the early stages of the afterglow phase, including a typical initial decay rate of 0.7 in the absence of external influences. The research reveals that the early decay rate of the afterglow phase is primarily determined by the interaction between radiation and matter, and that the proposed model can be used to predict the decay rates of the afterglow phase for events with limited data available for analysis.

Given a graph and a size parameter k, we can efficiently find two separate graphs with an added matching, where each has a complexity measure no greater than k, along with a matching of at least half the original graph's edges, within a runtime of 2's power of 14 times n cubed multiplied by k's power of 5.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to designing a gas-powered, self-sustaining, dual-legged robot capable of overcoming obstacles and overcoming limitations of battery-powered robots. Our proposed design utilizes a compressed air system to power the robot, offering numerous advantages over conventional battery-powered alternatives. We discuss the challenges associated with designing a gas-powered, dual-legged robot and outline the key components of our proposed design, including the compressed air system, hydraulic cylinders, and a microcontroller-based control system. We also discuss the benefits of our design, such as increased load-carrying capacity, extended operational time, and reduced maintenance costs. Our research contributes to the growing field of bipedal robots and offers a practical solution for industries that require heavy-duty, long-lasting, and efficient dual-legged robots.

In 1959, Heins posed the question of whether every valued domain with a Hamilton property possesses the H-property. This paper presents a solution to the initial part of the second question from [10], along with an examination of the Hamilton property and its relationship to the H-property. Additionally, we establish the equivalence of the H-property and the G-property, and provide a proof that the G-property is equivalent to the existence of a complete residue map.

HyperDegrade is a technique for managing dynamic energy efficiency in IoT
applications by balancing performance and energy consumption. It optimizes CPU
frequency adjustments to minimize energy usage while meeting performance targets,
even when performance requirements fluctuate. HyperDegrade takes into account
real-time system metrics, including the current application's performance,
available energy, and thermal constraints, to determine the most efficient CPU
frequency. The algorithm was implemented in the Linux kernel and tested on an
IoT device, showing significant improvements in energy efficiency compared to
existing methods. The results demonstrate that HyperDegrade can achieve up to
72% better energy efficiency than traditional approaches, while maintaining
acceptable performance levels.

This paper introduces a novel unknotting procedure for classical and welded links, building upon the conventional basis-unknotting method. Unlike the standard unknotting, this procedure allows for moves that preserve the welded knot type, which is not applicable in the standard context. As a direct consequence, it becomes evident that the welded unknotting number is at least as large as the usual unknotting number. Furthermore, the paper provides a way to calculate how these numbers relate to one another. Notably, this method enables the unknotting of the welded trefoil and other links within the welded category, which were previously considered permanently knotted under the standard context.

We demonstrate that the Fox-Hatcher loop constitutes a Vassiliev characteristic with a specific invariant value of three, thereby proving it is indeed a Vassiliev characteristic. Additionally, we identify another Vassiliev characteristic of order three and provide an illustration of the partial order between certain relevant infimum algebras of these newly discovered and previously known loop-based invariants.

We present a tactical multi-agent collaboration framework designed for a dynamic, uncertain environment, where a group of agents with limited computation and communication capabilities must navigate and identify hidden targets. Utilizing a Bayesian approach, we outline the conditions under which agents can effectively collaborate to locate these targets in a complex, changing environment.

This paper investigates privacy concerns in a new scenario for federated learning where multiple independent organizations collaborate to train a model without revealing their data. In this setting, known as "vertical federated learning," several data silos are joined to share information and improve a shared machine learning model. We examine the potential privacy risks associated with this approach, focusing on how participating entities can inadvertently expose sensitive information about one another during the training process. We demonstrate that common training methods can inadvertently reveal details about the algorithms and data of other participants. To mitigate these risks, we propose a framework that uses cryptographic techniques to protect the confidentiality of the data and algorithms used in this collaborative learning process. We provide concrete examples of this framework in the context of training a logistic regression model and show that it effectively prevents unauthorized access to the data and algorithms used in this process.

Traditional kernel estimation methods rely on fixed kernels, which are unalterable once determined and lack adaptability to specific data sets. In this study, we propose a novel approach to kernel estimation by developing random kernels that are uniquely tailored to individual data sets through pseudo random Fourier features. This approach allows us to estimate the optimal kernel in a computationally efficient manner by leveraging the positive definite nature of the resulting kernel matrix. We demonstrate the practical application of this method in support vector classification and regression, achieving superior performance compared to conventional estimators in simulated and real-world scenarios.

This research focuses on developing an efficient approach to map groups into space-filling shapes, specifically for groups composed of elements with $d$ dimensions, each having $k$ options. The proposed technique leverages the Wagner and Adams tree-based hashing method to create a digital representation of these groups, allowing for compact and fast mapping, particularly for large-scale groups. The underlying mathematics of this approach is explained in detail, and the effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through various tests, including comparisons with existing techniques. The results indicate that this approach can map extremely large groups into short binary codes, even for groups with high levels of complexity.

We prove that a conformally flat hypersurface within a sphere is necessarily a sphere itself, under the condition that the Mobius curvature in n-dimensions is non-positive. This dimension-specific result is stipulated for dimensions 4 and higher.

In next-generation wireless networks, multi-antenna systems are being utilized to deliver both information and power through the air interface. This paper investigates the optimal distribution of signal power in time-frequency domains when a base station transmits to multiple users, each with their own requirements for information and power. The goal is to maximize the utility function of data rates by carefully allocating resources, taking into account the non-linear relationship between received power and harvested energy. The problem is complex and involves finding a balance between utility and harvested energy, which can be solved using a two-step approach. The results show that the best signal processing technique for the base station is to use a linear precoder, and the resource allocation problem can be further simplified and solved efficiently. The paper provides valuable insights into the management of wireless resources to improve the performance of multi-user systems.

The structural composition of random graphs is characterized by statistical measures, including the distribution of branching factors for each node within the graph. A challenge in analyzing these distributions arises from the inherent variability in node degree, which can skew the data. A proposed method, maximum likelihood estimation, aims to accurately fit the branching factor distribution by treating observed data as a combination of node degree and branching factor distributions. A key finding reveals that an n-tree structure of a Cayley tree results in an avalanche-scale distribution of branching factors, with n being the scale of data observation. A n-free n-tree structure is indistinguishable from a standard tree structure, whereas an n-limited n-tree is equivalent to a truncated negative binomial distribution. A comparison with real-world data from a protein interaction network reveals that an n-free n-tree structure best represents the observed distribution.

Detecting high-frequency gravitational waves demands sensors with exceptional responsiveness in this frequency range. Traditional detectors, consisting of suspended mirrors, face limitations due to mechanical resonances of their optical components, which restrict their responsiveness beyond a few hundred Hertz. Researchers have proposed various enhancements, including advanced optical designs, to improve the responsiveness of these detectors at high frequencies. In this study, we demonstrate the benefits of a specific design, the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, which shows its potential for responsive performance in simulations. Furthermore, we show that integrating this design with other enhancements, such as fused-fiber membranes, could enable the detectors to achieve superior responsiveness, possibly even matching the performance of the proposed optimized detectors in terms of minimal movement in response to external forces in the high-frequency range.

In multi-user wireless networks, determining whether users' transmission areas overlap is crucial for efficient access control. In most existing methods, this is done by checking if users' signals are below a certain threshold. However, this approach can be unreliable in wireless networks with a very large number of antennas due to the difficulty of accurately estimating signal interference. This paper proposes a new access control protocol for such networks that uses the unique properties of transmission areas in these systems. It leverages the fact that transmission areas are shaped like donuts and that their shapes are highly resistant to changes in channel conditions. This protocol allows users to determine whether their transmission areas overlap with other users' areas, without needing to know the exact number of antennas or the interference levels. This approach is shown to be highly efficient in simulations, even in scenarios with a very large number of antennas.

Recent observations of young stellar objects have revealed submillimeter and millimeter-scale structures in their surrounding disks, which are primarily caused by variations in the opacity of dust. A potential explanation for these structures could be variations in the distribution of dust. To investigate this, we developed a radiative transfer model that incorporates radiation scattering and absorption, and used it to create a set of models based on a power-law gas density profile and various substructures in the dust opacity. Our model showed that a change in the dust opacity profile could create an over-dense region in the observed emission, and that the location of this region could be accurately predicted by the transition point in the dust opacity profile. We also found that a change in the scale of the dust opacity profile could create an under-dense region in the emission, which could be accurately predicted by the ratio of the scale to the size of the system. To further explore this, we used the radiative transfer model to create a set of models that included a transition in the dust opacity profile and found that the location of the over-dense region could be accurately predicted by a combination of the transition point and the scale of the system. We also found that the radiative transfer model could create an under-dense region in the emission that was wider than the scale of the system, which could be accurately predicted by the ratio of the scale to the size of the system. These results suggest that the radiative transfer model can be used to create a set of models

A novel tensor force, known as the $\sigma$-apple interaction, has been introduced in the Lagrangian of nucleons within nuclear physics. This force arises from the coupling of the $\sigma$ meson field to the orbital angular momentum of nucleons through their coupling to apple-shaped distortions of the scalar potential generated by the $A_1$ meson. Calculations using the relativistic mean-field approach with Big Apple interactions have been conducted to determine the properties of nuclei, revealing accurate predictions for semi-skewed nuclei' root-mean-square radii and binding energies. These calculations also highlight the Big Apple interaction's ability to accurately describe the density distribution of a neutron star and the equation of state for nuclear matter.

This research develops robust quantum logic gates based on the Molmer-Sorensen interaction within a system of trapped ions, focusing on minimizing sensitivity to frequency noise in trapped ions. By engineering the noise environment to ensure equal fluctuations in axial and radial motion frequencies, we demonstrate a significant reduction in gate error, potentially up to two orders of magnitude lower than conventional systems. The system's resistance to gate errors is examined across various noise environments and experimental parameters, revealing that typical noise levels could result in gate fidelities exceeding 99.99%. Furthermore, the system's scalability is assessed, showing that it can be applied to both current and future multi-qubit ion-trap processors.

Using the tight-binding model for a Dirac electron on a two-dimensional lattice, we derived an analytical solution for the linear dispersion segment, which allowed us to characterize the topological properties of the band structure, including the Berry phase and the Chern number. We found that the material's topology changes based on the parameter values, leading to either a quantum Hall effect or a Hall effect with zero quantization. The material exhibits a topological insulator state with a large Berry phase of 2π and time-reversal symmetry, and we calculated the orbital magnetic moment for non-relativistic electrons. Our study also established a connection between our model and the electronic behavior of the osmium-based material, HfIrOsTe$_4$, which exhibits a strongly coupled Dirac metal state.

The NA62 experiment at CERN has a high potential to significantly improve constraints on the coupling between electrons and neutral leptons with masses between 40 MeV and 1 GeV. By analyzing 10 years of data, the expected sensitivity to such neutral leptons can be achieved, with a 90% confidence level that would allow for the detection or exclusion of these hypothetical particles within a specific mass range. This level of achievement is based on an analysis of 820 picobarns of data, which is 10 times greater than what was actually collected during the experiment's run.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models in recent years, but our research indicates that for low-resource scenarios, a straightforward neural approach can effectively build upon a pre-existing $n$-gram language model. We investigate the underlying mechanisms of this residual learning process and find that the network primarily learns to predict the language distribution rather than the log-probabilities. We also discover that the network's ability to predict language distribution is constrained by its limited capacity to represent the underlying language distribution. To address this limitation, we propose a novel hybrid model that combines an $N$-gram language model with a restricted network that directly predicts the log-probabilities of the vocabulary. Our proposed model consistently outperforms both standalone models and residual learning of a softmax network in various text generation tasks.

In the complex task of aligning and reconstructing 3D faces from multiple faces in dark and obscured images, significant progress has been made in recent years. However, existing methods often focus on images containing a single face, neglecting the challenges posed by densely packed faces. Existing network-based solutions for multi-face scenarios are computationally expensive and lack precision in face-specific 3D face alignment and reconstruction. In response to these limitations, we introduce a novel, efficient, and effective self-supervised end-to-end framework called SADRNet for 3D face alignment and reconstruction in densely obscured faces images. The framework employs a novel self-alignment mechanism to enable a compact dual network to simultaneously predict 3D face alignment and reconstruction. The dual network leverages a shared backbone to reduce computational costs and a dual loss function to enhance reconstruction quality. The results of our experiments on the publicly available 3D Face Forensics++ dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in improving face detection accuracy by 11.4% and reducing reconstruction error by 0.014 mm on average.

The concept of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) is being revisited as a potential alternative to Dark Matter. A scalar field with two components is used in an inflationary model to generate a wide spectrum of curvature perturbations. The model is based on an inflationary potential that is linear and defined by two fields with a specific ratio $\alpha$. One field is linearly related to the ratio $\alpha$ of vacuum expectation values. The model is capable of being consistent with the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) data at small scales and the PBH constraints. A two-field version of the single-field $\alpha$-attractor model is proposed, in which an appropriate choice of parameters can lead to PBH formation. The model is shown to be consistent with the CMB data and the PBH constraints.

Consider a labeled, ordered tree with n nodes, where each node has a distinct label from 1 to n. We've identified the label with the highest vertical position, denoted as $d_1(T)$, within each tree T. The collective sum of these deepest labels across all possible labeled, ordered trees with n nodes is expressed as $d_n$. This total is expressed recursively, where $d_0$ equals 1 and for $n \geq 1$, $d_n$ equals the sum of $(i+1)$ multiplied by the product of $d_i$ and $d_{n-i-1}$, calculated for i ranging from 0 to $n-1$. This recursive formula can be simplified to represent the nth derivative of $\sec(x)$ with respect to x, evaluated at zero.

In recent local and national elections, numerous races and ballot measures have made counting ballots a complex task for election officials. This difficulty is compounded by the rising number of people who vote using paper ballots. Although scanning these ballots with an OCR machine is a common practice, it frequently encounters issues due to the irregular layout of ballot designs and the imperfections in printed text that result from various printing methods. This study introduces iOCR, an enhanced version of the standard OCR technology, which incorporates a linear regression model to improve the accuracy of recognizing numbers on ballots. iOCR achieved a 10% to 20% improvement in accuracy compared to the standard OCR when testing with sample ballots from 10 different municipalities. Furthermore, it successfully processed 90% of sample ballots from nine municipalities with an average error rate of less than 1%.
