The study of vector magnetic fields on the Sun's surface is essential for comprehending solar physics and predicting space weather. However, accurately measuring these fields is challenging due to the difficulty in directly observing magnetic vectors. Researchers rely on complex mathematical models, known as magnetochores, to infer these measurements from observable magnetic field scalars. These models, however, may introduce biases that could skew the data. In this paper, we investigate the sources and implications of bias in inferred measurements, specifically using a dataset of solar vector magnetic fields from the SOLIS/VSM instrument. We examine the relationship between the observed and inferred total field strengths, finding that the data exhibits significant deviations from linearity. Furthermore, we find that the models may inadvertently shape the distributions of observed fields, potentially hindering machine learning techniques used in space weather forecasting. To address this issue, we propose a straightforward calibration method that can be easily applied to existing datasets. This method yields more linear relationships and improved statistical correlations between the observed and inferred measurements. Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for model-induced biases in solar vector magnetic field data, which could have significant implications for research and forecasting.

Monte Carlo simulations in condensed matter physics frequently involve calculating the partition function through path integral formulations, yet a significant issue arises when fermionic systems with a negative determinant are encountered in certain path configurations. This "Hubbard sign dilemma" can lead to exponentially large fluctuations and hinder convergence in stochastic methods. We propose utilizing a complex-valued neural network to approximate the negative determinant within the variational Monte Carlo framework, effectively mitigating the "Hubbard sign dilemma". Our research demonstrates that even with an extremely large system and temporal lattice, our method successfully converges in a one-dimensional model, and achieves stable results in a spinless Hubbard model on a two-dimensional lattice.

Given a free monoid defined by a set of free generators and a non-degenerate endomorphism within that monoid, we define the concepts of topological entropy and factor complexity for specific words. Building upon these definitions, we investigate the properties of topological entropy and factor complexity in relation to changes in the free set of generators and the application of the non-degenerate endomorphism. It is established that the absolute differences between factor complexities of specific words under the given conditions are bounded, and the factor complexities of words with the same combinatorial structure are shown to be directly proportional. Similarly, the factor complexity of a word is equal to that of its root, and the factor complexity of the image of a word under the endomorphism is bounded by the factor complexity of the original word. Furthermore, it is proven that the topological entropy is invariant under the conditions of the free set of generators and the image of a word under the endomorphism has a topological entropy that is greater than or equal to that of the original word.

Pretrained language models excel at various natural language understanding tasks,
yet they often experience negative transfer when tackling unrelated tasks. In many
cases, these models perform poorly on tasks with little textual similarity to
their pretrained benchmarks. We investigate the impact of unsupervised retrieval
augmentation on a broad spectrum of NLU tasks, including textual entailment,
contradiction, question answering, and natural language inference. Contrary to
our expectations, we find that unsupervised retrieval enhancement can enable
models to generalize across different types of NLU problems to unrelated domains,
with little to no relation to their pretrained tasks. We further explore the
underlying mechanisms, demonstrating that models trained with unsupervised
retrieval enhancement are capable of identifying and focusing on crucial parts of
the input text, effectively mitigating the distraction of irrelevant text.

This research focuses on optimizing the privacy-preserving process of hyperparameter tuning in machine learning. By developing a theoretical framework, we establish a connection between private and non-private tuning, allowing for the application of conventional hyperparameter tuning methods. To address efficiency concerns, we introduce a sampling strategy for tuning that balances speed and accuracy. Additionally, we investigate the impact of various hyperparameter settings on private deep learning performance. Our empirical analysis reveals that privacy can significantly affect the optimal configuration of learning rate and batch size, with the most effective settings varying across different tasks. Through our experiments, we demonstrate the practical benefits of our approach, including the ability to identify learning rate and batch size configurations that substantially enhance the performance of private deep learning across multiple datasets.

This note explores the lattice of sub-distributions for a specific complex structure previously introduced, which has a similar nature to the Bruhat order within the symmetric group. We identify conditions under which the complex structure of the involutions within the symmetric group forms a distributive structure, and we also determine the modular properties of the complex structure.

A novel two-component model has been developed to analyze the elemental composition of 1,050 stars within the Milky Way's disk using a wide spectral range. This model, based on chemistry from aluminum to zinc, utilizes linear regression to isolate elemental patterns associated with geochemical processes and has outperformed traditional models by isolating these processes into distinct groups. As a result, the model has been applied to a larger dataset of 14,000 stars, revealing clear chemical groupings and trends linked to star formation processes and gas accretion patterns. These trends are most evident in elements with shorter geochemical timescales and vary across different wavelength ranges, with each range having its own degree of differentiation. Additionally, the model has identified a boundary between thick and thin disk populations that corresponds to the timescales of specific elements, with the outer disk exhibiting a unique distribution of star groups. The model has also revealed a relationship between the frequency of certain star groups and radial distance, with the "alpha plateau" group being most prevalent in the outer disk. Furthermore, the model has highlighted the presence of multiple formation sites within the outer disk and the influence of gas retention and loss patterns on the distribution of these sites.

This research focuses on examining the spread of rumors in China during the COVID-19 pandemic, specifically those circulated on WeChat public accounts. By analyzing 14 highly publicized rumors, the study categorizes their dissemination methods into four types based on their news sources and content, and assesses their impact through the number of readers they reached. Furthermore, it investigates the correlation between the number of readers and factors such as article titles, publication timing, views, and sharing rates. The findings reveal that official accounts with authoritative news sources tend to have a wider readership, and that posting times during weekdays, particularly in the afternoon, tend to attract more readers. The study offers valuable insights for creating effective public health messages and preventing the spread of misinformation.

A comprehensive understanding of the evolution of the local universe's galaxy populations can be achieved by studying planetary nebulae in detail. A significant challenge in using planetary nebulae to determine the distances to galaxies lies in the scarcity of well-studied PNe with precise redshift and distance measurements. A key aspect of the Fornax3D project involves developing a PNe database for galaxies within the Fornax cluster. A critical component of this effort is a PNe catalog for nine of these galaxies, which have a rich history of studying star formation. To accurately determine the distances to these galaxies, we need to identify PNe within them with precise redshifts. A novel, fully automated technique for extracting PNe from optical images was employed to extract data from the PHENIX integral field spectroscopy observations of these galaxies. By utilizing this technique, a PNe catalog was generated for each galaxy, which served as input for the distance determination method. A comprehensive analysis of the distances to these galaxies was then conducted, resulting in a set of precise, consistent, and reliable distance measurements for the nine galaxies within the Fornax cluster.

Mobile devices with powerful processors are commonly used for mobile applications that require real-time data handling. However, as these applications manage large, continuously updating datasets, they consume significant amounts of battery life. To address this issue, we present a specialized system called LifeStream, designed to operate on mobile devices and efficiently process data streams. LifeStream leverages the device's storage and processing capabilities to handle periodic flow operations, allowing it to run smoothly while minimizing energy usage. Our research shows that LifeStream can execute complex queries on datasets of up to 10GB in size and provides substantial performance improvements over existing solutions, even when considering the overhead of its scheduling framework.

This study establishes the characterization of timelike Bertrand curves within a Minkowski space, specifically deriving the relationship between the curvature functions of equivalent curves in a timelike space. It then derives the general form of curves that satisfy the Bertrand equivalence condition in a Minkowski space, and identifies and describes various types of timelike Bertrand curves, including those with constant curvature functions and those composed of null segments.

The choice of loss function in neural network training is a critical factor, yet its influence is not always straightforward to determine. In this research, we investigate the effects of loss function modification on a neural network's classification performance. We focus on two loss function variants - one that downweights over-confident predictions and another that prioritizes under-predictions. Through controlled experiments, we find that these loss function alternatives can be successfully used as proxies for the standard loss function, allowing us to identify network issues early in the training process. Moreover, we explore the potential of these loss function variants to directly guide the training of neural networks, and under specific conditions, we observe that they can lead to comparable performance to the network trained with the standard loss function.

The development of strain-induced crystallization in polymers is a complex process that involves multiple coupled phenomena, including thermomechanics and mass transfer. In this study, we investigate the coupled effects of these phenomena on microstructure formation in polybutadiene using numerical simulations. We focus on specific parameters, such as molecular weight, crystalline content, and local chain orientation, to better understand the resulting microstructure. Our simulations reveal that higher molecular weights lead to increased crystalline content and more pronounced chain orientation, whereas higher crystalline content results in more significant microstructure formation. We also find that the microstructure is most developed in regions of high strain, particularly in the necking region, and that the degree of microstructure formation is influenced by the rate of deformation. Overall, our research provides valuable insights into the microstructure formation of strain-induced crystalline polymers and highlights the importance of considering the interplay between molecular parameters and deformation rates.

To understand the mechanism behind the phase transition from nematic superconductivity to the normal state as temperature rises, we must examine two competing processes. The first involves the disruption of electron pairs within triplet Cooper couples due to their magnetic susceptibility, known as Pauli paramagnetism in the nematic state. In contrast, the second process entails the scattering of these couples by thermal fluctuations, leading to the creation of Nambu-Goldstone modes. We utilized the nematic triplet model to calculate the self-energy and the polarization vertex, which allowed us to determine the critical temperature for the transition from the superconducting state to the normal state. Our calculations show that the critical temperature is closely related to the energy scale of nematicity.

A key issue in CPM differential detection is that it converts frequency shifts into phase changes, introducing a detection delay that is proportional to the differential spacing and can cause significant performance degradation, especially in high-rate differential detection scenarios. To address this issue, we propose a novel low-complexity detection scheme called the extended differential partial response (EDPR) scheme, which expands the observation window and employs a set of filters to minimize processing delay. We demonstrate that the EDPR scheme achieves near-coherent detection performance with minimal processing overhead, and our simulation results show that it outperforms the conventional differential detection scheme, particularly for signals with high processing delay.

The concept of a cosmological event horizon is re-examined in an expanding universe, and a novel classification of regions within the universe is proposed. This new classification is based on the interplay between the Hubble parameter and the speed at which disturbances propagate in a vacuum. It is hypothesized that a vacuum behaves like a compressible fluid, exhibiting either quantum or thermodynamic stability in different regions. This leads to the proposal that the universe is divided into hot and cold thermal zones, separated by transition zones. It is further suggested that the thermal zones are permeable barriers through which heat can be transferred, and that the cosmic event horizon is not a universal feature, but rather a property of specific, localized regions. A model is developed to illustrate these concepts using a variable speed of sound in the context of cosmic structure formation. This model shows that the thermal zones can act as barriers to the formation of structures on a cosmic scale, and that the cosmic event horizon is a feature that arises only in certain regions of the model.

Recent advancements in large language models have enabled complex reasoning capabilities, yet their performance deteriorates significantly when handling intricate, logical rule-based systems. Researchers have developed training datasets incorporating natural language representations of logical knowledge to enhance reasoning skills, but these representations often lack a standardized, universal format. This paper introduces a novel knowledge format, Machine Common Knowledge (MCK), originally designed for digital systems, and creates an MCK representation of an expert system, known as the Atlas of Machine Common Knowledge (ATOMIC). This representation consists of a comprehensive set of production rules in natural language, sourced from over 100 existing knowledge bases. We incorporate the Atlas into our training data, along with other reasoning datasets, and evaluate the combined model's performance on the propositional reasoning tasks of bAbI tasks 25 and 26. Our results demonstrate that the Atlas achieves a perfect score of 100% on these tasks, whereas the previous best model, GPT-3, with 111 tokens context, only reached 80.2%.

Quantum computers are poised to revolutionize financial portfolio optimization, which is currently limited by the slow pace of classical computing. A particular class of quantum computers, known as Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum devices, presents a viable platform for addressing this challenge. However, their limited precision and susceptibility to errors pose significant obstacles. Our proposed NISQ-HHL algorithm, which integrates the HHL algorithm with a portfolio re-balancing strategy, aims to overcome these limitations and deliver a practical solution for real-world portfolio optimization on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum devices.

In order to enhance the performance of speech recognition systems, we have developed a novel attention-based multi-modal training method that leverages both audio and text data. Our approach utilizes dual attention mechanisms to identify and align the most significant parts of the corresponding sequences in text and speech. We have incorporated this focused representation into a multi-modal neural network training framework, allowing us to train robust recognition models using only aligned speech-text pairs. We have evaluated our approach on the Librispeech corpus and achieved comparable results to those obtained using randomly selected pairs, despite the challenges posed by the scarcity of manually transcribed pairs.

A natural extension of random parking problems involves assigning each car a uniformly random starting position within the interval [1,n]. In this context, the average number of cars that can successfully park in an infinite line has been found to approach 2/3 as n becomes very large, while the proportion of cars that can park in a limited line of n available spots converges to a specific value of approximately 0.304 as n approaches infinity.

We experimentally investigate the relationship between conductivity and quantum coherence in niobium nitride nanowires, focusing on how a gate electrode's influence varies with the thickness of the superconducting film. Our findings reveal that quantum phase-slips and Coulomb interactions are distinct phenomena that can be controlled independently. In particular, we observed that increasing the thickness of the nanowire reduces the impact of quantum phase-slips, while their effect on conductivity remains unchanged. This discovery highlights the unique characteristics of superconducting nanowires and their potential for quantum computing applications.

Predicting evolving scenes from surveillance videos is an essential task with significant practical applications. A key challenge in this task lies in accurately forecasting novel views that are not present in the available data. Our proposed approach, known as Innovative View Video Forecasting Utilizing a Dual Representation (I3V), tackles this challenge by leveraging two complementary sources of information: object trajectories and visual features. I3V represents object interactions through a graph-based framework and utilizes a multi-layered perceptron to capture the distinctive characteristics of innovative views. Experimental evaluations on two widely used datasets demonstrate the superiority of I3V over existing methods in terms of forecasting innovative views from video sequences.

As theoretical models continue to predict exotic inter-orbital phenomena, such as pairing and competition between different orderings, understanding these events requires new techniques. Inter-orbital pairing and ordering competition have been proposed but are challenging to measure due to the lack of straightforward analogues to established methods like ARPES and Bragg spectroscopy. Our research presents an innovative approach using ultracold atoms in a two-component system, where we employ two different energy bands to measure and characterize inter-orbital events. By applying a Feshbach resonance, we precisely tuned an inter-orbital pairing strength and measured its effects through Bragg spectroscopy, revealing the pairing gap and confirming our theoretical predictions through scanning tunneling microscopy.

This study focuses on the characteristics of the Omega baryon, a particle with three s quarks and -3 units of strangeness. Since its discovery in 1977 at Brookhaven National Laboratory, efforts have been made to identify this particle at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. A key aspect of research involves studying the full phase space of strange quarks, which is crucial for understanding the formation of hadrons made up of light and strange quarks in the early universe. A critical step in this analysis requires accurate knowledge of the Omega baryon's production cross section for both s and s' (or s, s' and s, s', s) charge exchange reactions.

Epidemiological modeling on urban transport networks is commonly simplified by assuming a well-mixed environment within each node, despite criticism of this approach's accuracy. This study investigates the utility of such a framework by training and evaluating agent-based and well-mixed models using data from a real urban bus route. Our findings reveal that the basic well-mixed framework effectively replicates infection transmission dynamics, performing comparably to the more complex agent-based model in predicting these outcomes.

We investigate the magnetic properties of cobalt layers made into multilayers with bismuth, specifically focusing on a key aspect - the size of the spin-orbit coupling that influences their behavior. As we adjust the cobalt layer thickness, we observe that the spin-orbit coupling can either increase or decrease, which hinders efforts to accurately predict its size. To address this, we developed a new approach that takes into account the impact of electrons bouncing off the edges of the multilayer, allowing us to precisely determine the spin-orbit coupling that affects their behavior. This method can be applied to other materials that exhibit similar properties.

This research paper presents fractional analogues of several generalized Mie-like potentials, including the generalized Hulthén, Yukawa, and Rosen-Morse potentials, within a higher-dimensional framework. It then applies a modified Jumarie type fractional Laplacian to a time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation, specifically for a particle confined to a higher-dimensional space. By employing the Nikiforov-Uvarov method, the paper derives the corresponding fractional eigenfunctions and fractional energy eigenvalues for these potentials. It is found that these fractional energy eigenvalues are complex numbers, and the derived fractional energy eigenvalues are shown to be consistent with previous research.

We investigate the use of Lipschitz consistency as a form of regularization for deep neural networks, particularly in scenarios where there is noisy data. By enforcing the confidence levels of our network to decrease as the distance between inputs increases, we can improve the robustness of the network to noisy labels. We develop a consistent consistency loss that aligns with the proposed distance metric, and we demonstrate through our experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, using both ResNet and VGG network architectures, that this method effectively enhances the generalization performance of the networks. Furthermore, we find that the benefits of this approach are most pronounced when the level of label noise is relatively high.

We investigate the production of a Drell-Yan pair of quarks in third-generation gauge vector leptoquark models to a higher level of accuracy. Our calculations consider the impact of next-to-leading order QCD corrections, taking into account real-emission processes, virtual corrections, and various sources of uncertainty. In addition, we developed a modified parton shower algorithm to better simulate radiation patterns in this process. Our results indicate that a significant level of accuracy can be achieved in modeling Drell-Yan pair production, with implications for distinguishing between different types of leptoquark models at future colliders.

In medical imaging, particularly with Positron Emission Tomography (PET), increasing the radiation dose by acquiring more data improves image quality but is undesirable. A common alternative, CT-guided PET, leverages CT images to enhance PET quality at lower doses. However, this approach is limited by its dependence on deep learning, which struggles when encountering new types of PET images not present in the training data. This research introduces a novel, robust, low-dose PET reconstruction method that maintains performance even with unfamiliar images. By utilizing a generative model and a carefully selected training dataset, it achieves a balance between improved reconstruction at higher doses and reduced performance when the images are not well-represented in the training data. A key feature of this approach is the estimation of uncertainty, allowing it to automatically adjust the reliance on the generative model based on the images' novelty. This uncertainty-aware learning framework is implemented using a flexible variational inference method, enabling efficient, end-to-end training. The proposed approach is validated on multiple datasets, including the high-dose PHANTOM and low-dose PET/MRI data from the Mayo Clinic, demonstrating its ability to achieve accurate reconstructions with reliable uncertainty estimates.

This theory, developed by Robin Cooper in 1991, is a linguistic approach that links pronouns to their corresponding nouns within a text. This research integrates centering theory into a baseline neural coreference resolution model, using mathematical relations and linguistic category constraints to enhance the system's performance. Accurately determining the distance between two points indoors using WiFi signals is a challenging task. The approach involves collecting signal strength data at known distances, training an artificial neural network, and then using the trained model to predict distances based on new measurements. An in-depth analysis of the beam disruption instability (BDI) requires filling configuration dependence in an energy recovery linac (ERL). This research focuses on a mathematical model describing the behavior of polymer bristles with intricate patterns, taking into consideration molecular extension in detailed shape configurations. A subgraph within a graph G is considered resolving if, when mapped to the graph's vertices, it uniquely determines the position of each node based on its shortest distance to the subgraph. A research team from the University of Haifa used Python to process the Fermi-LAT data, which covers the entire sky, from 2008 to 2020, with an energy range of 100 MeV to 820 GeV. We introduce the Interacting and Leading in Dungeons and Dragons (IALDD) dataset, an interactive role-playing game (RPG) scenario featuring a human player and an AI Dungeon Master (DM). This dataset encompasses 1000 recorded RRP games, incorporating a unique set of DM-centric questions designed to probe the Theory of Mind (ToM) of the Dungeon Master. We examine the implications of this dataset for advancing artificial general intelligence (AGI) and provide guidance for training and developing models to excel in the IALDD challenges. Our research reveals that even the latest state-of-the-art language models struggle to demonstrate ToM in their interactions. We also explore the use of the IALDD dataset for a broader spectrum of applications beyond Theory of Mind, such as natural language understanding, commonsense reasoning, and multi-turn dialogue.

A primary focus in the study of complex protein knots is understanding how their intricate topological structures influence function and folding. While experimental and theoretical approaches have been utilized to analyze the folding dynamics of complex protein knots, a lesser-explored aspect of this issue is the effect of their intricate topological structures on their folding pathways. In this study, a random ensemble of two-state protein models with complex knots was generated, and a topological measure was developed to identify the ensemble's preferred states and potential pathways for folding. This development revealed that the ensemble's intricate topological structure constrains its state space, resulting in a preference for self-crossing-free configurations that can be characterized as "loose" or "tight" depending on their spatial arrangement. Furthermore, the study found that the ensemble's folding process follows a deterministic pathway from loose to tight configurations, which aligns with the folding process observed in native states of complex protein knots in reality.

To improve the counterfactual reasoning skills of large language models, we developed a novel framework called DISCO, which leverages the self-correction capabilities of these models. To make the counterfactuals consistent with the prompt architecture, we applied three correction techniques: extracting explanations, modifying word order, and adjusting the phrasing. Our experiments show that pre-trained model architectures can effectively self-correct and that the phrasal counterfactuals provide a more reliable assessment for guiding further optimization.

The unique atomic arrangement of graphene can facilitate remote epitaxy, allowing for the growth of high-quality crystalline films without the need for van der Waals epitaxy, which often restricts the composition of Heusler films due to lattice mismatch with traditional substrates. This study compares remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy in the growth of Heusler films on graphene and sapphire substrates, revealing that remote epitaxy can produce a wider range of balanced Heusler compositions than previously thought. The study also demonstrates that the quality of graphene and the resulting pinholes can significantly impact the composition of the resulting films, and that remote and van der Waals epitaxy can coexist in the same growth process. Ultimately, this research highlights the potential of remote epitaxy to produce a broader range of balanced Heusler compositions than previously possible with van der Waals epitaxy.

A code is considered $\mathbb{Z}_p$-linear if it forms a module over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ with a rank that equals its size multiplied by the logarithm of $p$. In this article, we investigate code properties specifically for $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, which are constructed from the direct sum of two free $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-modules and have a total rank of $2p$. The primary objective is to establish a $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-basis for the coset leader table, thereby facilitating efficient decoding of linear and non-linear codes. The article also delves into the concept of the dimension of the null space of a code, which is defined as the logarithm of its size multiplied by the logarithm of $p$. The article provides a comprehensive overview of the code's properties, including its distance profile, minimum distance, and dual code.

Supervising deep learning models with single positive labels leads to them learning to identify positive instances, but also results in models mistaking parts of negative data for the intended targets. This phenomenon, where the model treats negative samples as having a single positive label, can be beneficial as it enables the training and deployment of deep learning models in scenarios where only a fraction of negative data is labeled. This paper delves into the underlying causes of this behavior, presents evidence that the model is indeed extracting meaningful information from negative data, and demonstrates the utility of reusing such instances for training and evaluation.

We establish a 2-categorical framework for finite-dimensional quantum mechanics, demonstrating a left adjoint to the functor that maps Hilbert spaces to symmetric monoidal categories with a duality structure. This adjunction provides a connection between the observable properties and behavior of a quantum system, represented by a symmetric monoidal category with a duality structure, and its corresponding Hilbert space. This relationship can be interpreted as the quantum version of the fact that the structure of an object within a category provides insight into the object's properties and behavior. This 2-categorical approach to quantum mechanics is explored in the main text of the paper, with a discussion of the implications of this framework.

The energy source behind gamma-rays observed from galaxies at high frequencies remains uncertain. We propose that high-energy gamma-rays in nearby galaxies can be generated by protons trapped in magnetic fields of rapidly spinning, dense disks located at the center of galaxies. We focus on the galaxy NGC 4258, whose central disk has well-documented characteristics, and show that gamma-rays at mid-energies can be produced by protons trapped in its magnetic fields. We then conduct an in-depth analysis of the relationship between the gamma-rays and the water emissions observed in the galaxy, and find that the gamma-rays are more abundant in areas with less intense water emissions. We also conduct a statistical study of gamma-rays and water emissions in 10 other galaxies with similar features, and find that the gamma-rays tend to be more abundant in areas with lower water emissions. We conclude that the gamma-rays are generated by protons trapped in magnetic fields of rapidly spinning, dense disks located at the center of galaxies.

This research paper addresses the challenge of categorizing heart sounds into normal and abnormal classes under noisy conditions. The study explores various noise types and intensities, as well as physical distortions that may occur during the recording process. A range of deep learning models, including convolutional neural networks and fully connected networks, are evaluated to determine the most effective approach for categorizing heart sounds. The research also introduces an additive noise model that realistically simulates the recording process, taking into account the potential transmission of background noise to the recording. The study's results are presented in terms of accuracy, with the best model achieving a high level of success in distinguishing between normal and abnormal heart sounds under various conditions.

The rapid expansion of the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) has created significant challenges related to data privacy and interoperability. These issues pose a potential threat to the widespread adoption of IoMT in medical settings. To overcome these obstacles, a wearable medical device has the potential to leverage transfer learning and a federated learning approach to enhance its diagnostic capabilities. Specifically, a wearable device can collect a large amount of personal health data locally and collaborate with multiple medical institutions to jointly train a shared model. In this paper, we introduce FedHealth, a novel framework that combines transfer learning and a federated learning approach for wearable medical devices. FedHealth enables a wearable device to work with multiple medical institutions to jointly train a shared model, thereby improving its diagnostic accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that FedHealth significantly outperforms traditional machine learning methods in terms of F1-score and accuracy, achieving an improvement of up to 10%. Furthermore, FedHealth has shown remarkable efficiency in terms of training time, reducing the training duration by up to 90%.

This paper investigates the relationship between portfolio performance metrics, specifically mean and skewness of returns, and advanced optimization methodologies used in quantitative finance. By reviewing established models such as mean-variance, semi-variance, CVaR, and Gini's delta, we explore their applications in portfolio management. We then introduce a novel framework that incorporates both return skewness and kurtosis into the traditional variance optimization technique. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this enhanced model through numerical simulations and real-world data, highlighting its ability to accurately reflect portfolio performance.

Researchers are using pulsar timing arrays to detect gravitational waves originating from supermassive binary systems. To identify these signals effectively, it's crucial to optimize computational resources while maintaining high precision in modeling. In this work, the precision of various post-Newtonian approximations for generalizing pulsar binaries' motions from elliptical to circular orbits is evaluated. The precision of these approximations is compared, and their computational efficiency is assessed. The results reveal that a specific combination of modeling techniques offers the most precise and computationally efficient solution. This optimal approach offers a 10% precision improvement over other methods, a significant advantage given the high dimensionality of data being analyzed. The ongoing global pandemic caused by the novel coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) has led to a surge in the use of mathematical epidemiological models. These models are valuable tools for comprehending the epidemic's dynamics, assessing control measures, and forecasting the spread of the virus. However, the diversity of model structures employed to study the outbreak highlights the need for a unified approach. In this review, we examine the underlying assumptions and limitations of various model types, discuss the implications of these models for policy-making, and outline the key components that should be incorporated in the next generation of epidemiological models.

Researchers have examined how a small number of atoms interact when a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate forms molecules through the process of association. This interaction involves three-body recombination, where three atoms come together, and has been theoretically and computationally studied using a specific model that takes into account both interatomic forces and a molecule's distinct mass and interaction properties. The study found that ignoring the molecule's characteristics can lead to significant errors in predicting how these interactions evolve over time. However, accurately modeling them allows for the prediction of a unique phenomenon where a condensate can suddenly become a mixture of atoms and molecules due to an intense loss of atoms, leading to a runaway effect. The theory has been validated through numerical simulations and can be applied to a real-world experiment involving sodium atoms.

A novel data storage technology, DNA, has been proposed to potentially revolutionize data storage due to its vast capacity and low cost. However, a significant issue with this technology is that it relies heavily on hierarchical structures and data verification, both of which require extensive data processing and manipulation. A new cryptographic scheme, called Hierarchy and Data Refreshing Efficiently (HiDeRe), has been developed to address this challenge by providing secure and efficient hierarchical data management and refreshment. This scheme allows for a client to delegate file storage to a server with a hierarchical structure, while ensuring data confidentiality, integrity, and availability. HiDeRe provides four main functionalities, including dynamic file access control, proof of storage, integrity verification, and a method for refreshing encrypted files and the underlying hierarchical structure. By combining these functionalities, HiDeRe enables the client to outsource file management to the server while maintaining full control over data security and management.

Our novel hybrid approach seamlessly integrates the discrete exterior calculus framework for the shallow water equations with a deep neural network architecture, resulting in a robust solver capable of handling complex, irregular geometries and highly variable topographies. Our method employs polynomial approximations to represent physical quantities and geometric configurations, allowing for efficient solution of the shallow water equations on irregular domains through a streamlined set of ordinary differential equations. Our results demonstrate our solver's exceptional speed and accuracy, achieving up to four orders of magnitude faster solution times than traditional numerical methods while maintaining high levels of precision. Our research also highlights the potential for our approach to handle an exceptionally wide range of Froude numbers with consistent precision. Our flexible framework is adaptable to other fluid dynamics problems, making our approach a versatile tool for researchers and practitioners alike.

HDR photography aims to capture a wider range of brightness levels than conventional photography by taking multiple photos at different exposure settings and merging them into a single image. Although the technique is well-established, automating the process remains a challenge, particularly on mobile devices. In this project, we develop an algorithm to automate HDR photography by determining the ideal exposure settings and combining the captured images. The algorithm selects a series of settings that optimize image quality while minimizing the risk of over-saturation and focusing, and uses a deblur approach to merge the images. The results of this approach are showcased in images captured with a mobile device.

Integrating causal analysis with deep learning has gained popularity in recent years, particularly in areas like representation learning and model interpretation. However, a significant challenge arises in training neural networks to understand causality due to the vast and complex parameter space that governs causal relationships. To address this issue, we propose a new framework called Causal Network Navigation (CNN), which enables standard feed-forward neural networks to learn and interpret directed causal connections between input features. By equipping these networks with the ability to traverse a graph representing possible causal pathways, we allow them to derive an initial association between features and subsequently refine their understanding through an innovative meta-learning approach. Our results from various experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that CNN pre-training significantly enhances the network's capacity to capture meaningful causal connections. Moreover, we show that the network's internal representation of these connections aligns with human reasoning, providing a more transparent and explainable artificial intelligence system.

We introduce a new variant of the b-principle tailored for symplectic manifolds that possess very little capacity, establishing a fundamental rule in symplectic topology. This enhanced b-principle subsequently enables the resolution of the second part of the famous Mumford conjecture, which concerns the topological properties of moduli spaces of Riemann surfaces. Specifically, it allows us to prove that the space of Lagrangian submanifolds in a torus is topologically equivalent to the torus itself, in a category that considers Lagrangian submanifolds and Hamiltonian transformations.

This study compares multilevel preconditioners for solving cardiac mechanics finite element problems, focusing on their scalability on complex, irregular meshes. We examine geometric-based methods, including MiniV-cycle and geometric multigrid (GMG), as well as a spectrum of problem-based alternatives, such as physics-informed multigrid, Newton-Krylov multigrid, and multilevel preconditioned minimal residual method. Our research utilizes a realistic 3D model of the human heart, and our multilevel preconditioners are implemented using the deal.II finite element library in conjunction with the AMGCL multigrid package. Our findings reveal that geometric multigrid methods are highly scalable and efficient, particularly when utilizing ILU0 or multilevel ILU (MLILU) fill-in elimination strategies. Moreover, we find that problem-based multigrid methods are highly comparable to their geometric counterparts in terms of performance.

We examine the diffusion of a tracer particle through various complex media, focusing on models where the underlying medium's permeability follows different non-Gaussian random distributions, specifically power laws and log-normal distributions. The diffusion process is described using the Fokker-Planck equation, and its solution reveals the mean squared displacement of the particle over time. Interestingly, the diffusion process exhibits non-Gaussian behavior, characterized by a time-independent lambda that varies depending on the distribution parameters. The lambda value is found to be greater than one, indicating non-Gaussian diffusion. Theoretical predictions are validated through numerical simulations of the stochastic process. The research has implications for understanding the transport of particles in diverse environments, including porous media, biological tissues, and granular materials.

A comprehensive mathematical framework is developed to describe the spatial distribution of light in optical systems with a specific geometry, taking into account linear and Kerr nonlinear light-matter interactions. This framework is applicable to analyzing light patterns in integrated photonic circuits and ring resonators. The study derives explicit formulas for spatial light distributions in waveguides and explains their properties, including the impact of the Kerr effect on light patterns, which can lead to bistability and hysteresis. A method is also presented to calculate the coupling between spatial modes in waveguides due to nonlinearity, which can be used to predict integrated photonic device behavior. A particular application of this theory is explored in detail, focusing on all-optical switches consisting of waveguides and resonators. The device's performance is characterized by parameters such as the extinction ratio, power consumption, and length of the device, which can be predicted using the universal theory.

A primary goal in fluid dynamics research is to understand and master turbulent flows, yet accurately simulating and measuring turbulent flows at higher Reynolds numbers remains a significant challenge. Due to limitations in experimental flow measurements, high-resolution data is often unavailable, posing a challenge in studying turbulent flows at these higher Reynolds numbers. A generative adversarial network-based method has been developed to restore high-resolution data from lower-resolution data, effectively recovering velocity fluctuations at different Reynolds numbers (150, 250, and 400) from 200-resolution data at the same locations. This model was trained using direct simulation data and successfully restored velocity fields with lower errors than linear interpolation methods. A key finding is that the model can restore velocity fields at Reynolds numbers not included in its training, demonstrating its potential utility in experimental settings where high-resolution data may be inaccessible.

L2Explorer is a novel simulation platform designed for training and evaluating reinforcement learning agents in dynamic, changing worlds. Unlike traditional learning environments, this platform accounts for a variety of real-life scenarios where the rules and parameters of the learning task shift over time. It provides a comprehensive set of settings and evaluation methods for studying reinforcement learning in such complex, ever-changing contexts. The developers of L2Explorer also conducted a detailed analysis of the challenges and potential breakthroughs in lifelong learning, and highlighted the key components of this approach. As a result, Reinforcement Learning experts and scholars working on lifelong learning can utilize L2Explorer as a versatile tool for exploring and advancing their respective fields.

Human-in-the-loop (HITL) applications are particularly suitable for complex processes that involve multiple, diverse steps and are often too complicated to fully specify beforehand. In this context, we introduce a novel HITL approach for processes represented as sequences of actions, where a special type of participant, the explorer, takes on the role of initiating processes, executing steps, and pausing for input from other participants who provide additional information or knowledge. Our approach utilizes a formalism called processes over streams, which model dynamic processes that incorporate a declarative component consisting of rules that can be added or modified by participants at any time. We enhance the existing process execution model with a new control algorithm, the Control-Explorer, which determines when to halt and seek input from participants. To illustrate the practical utility of our approach, we provide a proof-of-concept implementation and a real-world case study involving the intricate process of creating a comic book.

This paper provides an overview of compactifications of moduli spaces from both an algebraic geometry and a representation theory perspective.
